sources.text: Dapagliflozin in Patients with Heart Failure and Reduced Ejection Fraction. BACKGROUND: In patients with type 2 diabetes, inhibitors of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) reduce the risk of a first hospitalization for heart failure, possibly through glucose-independent mechanisms. More data are needed regarding the effects of SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with established heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction, regardless of the presence or absence of type 2 diabetes. METHODS: In this phase 3, placebo-controlled trial, we randomly assigned 4744 patients with New York Heart Association class II, III, or IV heart failure and an ejection fraction of 40% or less to receive either dapagliflozin (at a dose of 10 mg once daily) or placebo, in addition to recommended therapy. The primary outcome was a composite of worsening heart failure (hospitalization or an urgent visit resulting in intravenous therapy for heart failure) or cardiovascular death. RESULTS: Over a median of 18.2 months, the primary outcome occurred in 386 of 2373 patients (16.3%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 502 of 2371 patients (21.2%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.85; P<0.001). A first worsening heart failure event occurred in 237 patients (10.0%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 326 patients (13.7%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.59 to 0.83). Death from cardiovascular causes occurred in 227 patients (9.6%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 273 patients (11.5%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.69 to 0.98); 276 patients (11.6%) and 329 patients (13.9%), respectively, died from any cause (hazard ratio, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.71 to 0.97). Findings in patients with diabetes were similar to those in patients without diabetes. The frequency of adverse events related to volume depletion, renal dysfunction, and hypoglycemia did not differ between treatment groups. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction, the risk of worsening heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes was lower among those who received dapagliflozin than among those who received placebo, regardless of the presence or absence of diabetes. (Funded by AstraZeneca; DAPA-HF ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03036124.).

Heart Failure 1941-3289 1941-3297 <?publisher_abbrev wolters?> pmc-is-collection-domain yes pmc-collection-title Lippincott Open Access PMC12704667 PMC12704667.1 12704667 12704667 41170566 10.1161/CIRCHEARTFAILURE.125.013496 CIRCHF-2025-013496D 1 3 10021 10162 Original Articles Survival Odds to Minimize Risk Heterogeneity Bias in Heart Failure Trials: Application to Dapagliflozin https://orcid.org/0000-0002-2974-2003 Myte Robin PhD In an adequately sized randomized clinical trial with a parallel group design in a relatively risk-homogeneous population, measured and unmeasured patient characteristics at baseline will generally be well balanced between treatment groups, with balance maintained with time, leading to unbiased estimates of the treatment effects. In populations with high risk heterogeneity, however, effective treatments tend to retain more high-risk patients at risk in the active therapy group, while the placebo group becomes depleted of these patients over time, leading to postrandomization selection bias in hazard ratios (HRs) derived from Cox regression. 2 – 4 If heterogeneity in risk is unexplained by measured baseline characteristics, statistical analyses cannot fully adjust for differences among patients remaining at risk in the treatment versus the placebo group. In fact, because the HR compares the instantaneous event risk among patients who have not yet had an event, postrandomization selection bias is inherent to its definition—meaning a treatment that prolongs survival does not necessarily reduce the hazard at every time point. 5 , 6 In this study, we evaluate a potential solution to risk heterogeneity: analysis of time-to-first end points using the semiparametric survival proportional odds model (SPOM). 7 , 8 This method assumes converging hazards between treatment groups but still produces a single treatment effect measure independent of time—the survival odds ratio (SOR). The main appeal of the SPOM is its ability to provide consistent and clinically interpretable treatment effect estimates even when hazards are not proportional, although maintaining much of the framework of the widely used Cox regression by simply replacing the proportional hazards assumption with a similar assumption on proportional odds. Our study aims to compare SPOM and Cox regression under conditions of varying risk heterogeneity using both simulations and data from 2 recent heart failure trials—DAPA-HF (Dapagliflozin in Patients With Heart Failure and Reduced Ejection Fraction) and DELIVER (Dapagliflozin in Heart Failure With Mildly Reduced or Preserved Ejection Fraction). 9 – 11 Our findings indicate that SPOM is more robust to heterogeneity compared with Cox, resulting in less attenuation of treatment effect estimates and greater statistical power in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) trials. Methods Data underlying the findings described in this article can be obtained in accordance with AstraZeneca’s data sharing policy described at https://astrazenecagrouptrials.pharmacm.com/ST/Submission/Disclosure . Cox Proportional Hazards Model The enduring popularity of the Cox proportional hazards model—or Cox regression—in clinical trials is likely due to the numerous advantages it offers: Distribution-free method: Cox regression does not require assumptions about the form of the unknown distributions for estimation purposes. Minimal assumptions: besides the common assumption of noninformative censoring found in many survival analysis methods, Cox regression requires only the proportionality of hazards to be satisfied. A single summary measure: it provides a single summary measure, the HR, which quantifies the treatment effect across the entire duration of the follow-up without the need to specify a time point for evaluation. A close connection between the Cox regression with a single covariate with the nonparametric log-rank test. This allows for a straightforward calculation of the statistical power, based only on the required number of events. The test is optimal under the proportionality of hazards assumption. 12 When the proportionality of hazards assumption is violated in a meaningful way—notably in the presence of unexplained risk heterogeneity—several alternatives to Cox regression can be considered. Generally, these alternatives resolve the nonproportionality issue but introduce other complexities. For example, some models may require additional distributional assumptions (such as parametric distributions, for example, the negative binomial regression applied to a single event) or produce treatment effect estimates that are time-dependent, thus, cannot be summarized with a single summary measure. One such time-dependent alternative is the Restricted Mean Survival Time model. 13 This model provides a single summary measure from a distribution-free estimation; however, the estimate depends on the timepoint of evaluation, which limits its generalizability, similar to a milestone analysis comparing percentages of patients with an event at a given timepoint. Specifically, such milestone analyses disregard data after the selected milestone. The milestone should be specified in advance with no clear method for its selection, and the impact of the milestone on the analysis can be substantial. 14 Longer timeframes of evaluation will provide larger treatment effects, even if the event rates in both groups are constant over time. Survival Proportional Odds Model The SPOM addresses the issue of nonproportional hazards without introducing additional complexities. 7 , 8 , 15 By substituting the proportional hazards assumption with the assumption of proportional survival odds, SPOM naturally allows hazard functions to converge over time—a feature implicitly built into the model. Like Cox regression, the method remains distribution-free and provides a single, interpretable summary measure—the SOR—that captures the treatment effect over the entire study follow-up. Therefore, the SPOM preserves advantages 1 to 3 listed above of the Cox regression listed above (for bullet point 4 and the considerations of the statistical power, see below). The SOR also has additional advantages: It is a causal treatment effect measure since it is based on the comparison of survival functions. On the contrary, the HR does not have a causal interpretation (with the exception of no treatment effect or an unverifiable assumption of independent counterfactual event times is met 4 ). The SOR can be interpreted as the ratio of odds of being event-free in the active group compared with the control group. Conversely, 1/SOR represents the ratio of odds of experiencing an event. Similar to an HR, a value of 1/SOR below 1 indicates a positive treatment effect, a value of 1 indicates no effect, and values above 1 indicate harm. The HR is often interpreted in terms of risk reduction, for example, HR=0.8 is interpreted as a 20% risk reduction in experiencing an event. This interpretation is not technically correct, since the hazard rate is the probability that a patient who has survived up to a certain time will experience the event in the next instant. On the contrary, 1/SOR is directly linked to the odds of experiencing an event (Figure ). Hence, 1/SOR=0.8 is clearly a 20% reduction in the odds of experiencing an event. For example, if the survival probability in the control arm at the end of follow-up is 80%, the odds of an event in the control arm are 4 to 1. A 20% reduction in the odds of an event results in a 5 to 1 odds of an event in the active arm. Therefore, when communicating the results of the analyses, it is more intuitive to describe an increase in the odds of remaining event-free rather than to explain a reduction in hazard. The SOR is more directly related to Kaplan-Meier survival estimates, which estimate the survival probabilities over time, the most common visualization of treatment effects in outcome trials, and an estimate of the SOR is derivable directly from such figures (see Figure )—which is not true for HRs. Figure 1. Illustration of survival odds as an efficacy summary measure in a clinical trial. Survival odds are directly tied to survival probabilities, typically estimated with the Kaplan-Meier method, and reflect the odds of being event-free by a given time point. In contrast, hazard represents the risk of an event among patients still event-free at each moment; this concept is more abstract, is only indirectly related to survival curves, and differences in patient risk at randomization lead to a selection of less sick patients over time, which can bias comparisons between groups. We generated individual patient data from typical HF 1:1 randomized trials of up to 4000 patients followed for 3 years. The event times in each treatment group were simulated assuming separate Weibull distributions with distinct scale and shape parameters—allowing for nonproportional hazards between groups. Parameter values were chosen to represent multiple scenarios spanning different levels of risk heterogeneity, informed by Weibull parameters estimated in DAPA-HF and DELIVER trial data (see Table S1 ). For each scenario, we simulated 1000 trials. In each simulated trial, we estimated treatment effects using Cox regression (HR) and SPOM (1/SOR). We then assessed statistical power for each method as the proportion of the 1000 simulated trials in which a statistically significant effect was detected (1-sided alpha=0.025) and also evaluated type 1 error. Analyses of Real Clinical Trials To compare SPOM and Cox methods, we reanalyzed 2 real heart failure trials of dapagliflozin—the DAPA-HF and DELIVER trials. For the primary end point in each trial of time to first worsening of heart failure or cardiovascular death, we calculate the Kaplan-Meier curves with different fitted parametric proportional and nonproportional hazards models corresponding to underlying assumptions of common primary analysis models ( Table S2 ). We estimated treatment effects as HRs using Cox regression and as SOR or 1/SOR for comparability using SPOM, both models adjusted for the trials’ stratification factor of type 2 diabetes status. We also evaluated the statistical power of each model by repeatedly bootstrapping resampling the data from each trial 1000 ×, rerunning the analysis for each resample, and then calculating how often each method detected a statistically significant treatment effect (using a 1-sided alpha level of 0.025). All statistical analyses were performed in R (version 4.1.0), using the survival package for Cox regression and the timereg package for SPOM analyses. Both the DAPA-HF and DELIVER trials were approved by institutional review committees at each trial center, and all participants provided written informed consent. Results Figure shows Kaplan-Meier curves for the primary end point in each trial with different fitted parametric proportional and nonproportional hazards models. For the DAPA-HF trial conducted in the heart failure with reduced ejection fraction population, even the simplest exponential family offers a good conformity with the Kaplan-Meier estimates, suggesting that the heart failure with reduced ejection fraction population is relatively homogeneous (Figure A). In contrast, the HFpEF population (DELIVER) provides a different illustration (Figure B). The active treatment group maintained a constant incidence rate, whereas the control group experienced an increased incidence rate for the first one and a half years, followed by a curve bend and a convergence of the control Kaplan-Meier curve with the active curve. This figure suggests the occurrence of postrandomization selection bias, where the patients in the control group become less frail over time, causing the Kaplan-Meier curves for both groups to draw closer together over time than their initial separation. For nonproportional hazards models, the nonparametric Kaplan-Meier curves are well approximated by a parametric Weibull distribution with different shape parameters in both groups (the exponential distribution, that is, Weibull with shape parameter 1, fitting the active group reasonably well). This indicates violations of both the proportionality of hazards and the proportionality of odds assumptions. Figure illustrates the true cumulative incidence of our 4 simulation scenarios. Scenarios 1 and 2 provide cases of low heterogeneity where the incidence rate in active and control groups is either constant (scenario 2) or almost constant (scenario 1). Scenarios 3 and 4 provide cases of large heterogeneity and, as a consequence, converging survival curves (and hence, converging hazards). Figure S1 provides comparisons between 1/SOR versus the HR over time for these 4 scenarios. For low heterogeneity cases, the 1/SOR is numerically either very close to or slightly above the HR over time. This means that no or numerically lower overall treatment effect estimate of 1/SOR (average survival ratio over time) is expected compared with the average HR. Therefore, since the SPOM usually has a higher SE than the HR from the Cox regression, the SPOM will have lower statistical power than the Cox regression in low heterogeneity populations. Figure 3. On the contrary, for scenarios 3 and 4, we see that over time, the HR is increasing more rapidly than 1/SOR. Although larger heterogeneity increases both estimates, the HR is increasing faster than 1/SOR. Therefore, although the 1/SOR has a higher SE, it is expected that low attenuation of the treatment effect will result in higher power for the SPOM in highly heterogeneous populations. This is demonstrated in Figure , where the increase in power of the SPOM compared with the Cox model is apparent as the heterogeneity of the population increases. Treatments effective in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction populations often failed to demonstrate efficacy in HFpEF populations, sometimes narrowly missing statistical significance for the primary end point. Although there may be mechanistic reasons why a treatment may work at the lower range of ejection fraction but not at the higher ends, the statistical methods used, specifically the time-to-first event analysis with the Cox proportional hazards model, may also be a contributing factor. Power improvements have been shown in the reanalysis of HFpEF trials using models not based on HR. 1 In response to these challenges, some contemporary HFpEF trials have started using total event end points as primary end points. 16 It is often assumed that total event analyses provide higher statistical power, as they incorporate more events, including not only the first events of patients but also recurrent events. However, this is not always the case. 17 Total event end points may yield a wider CI than time-to-first event end points owing to a more complex SE structure than Cox regression. Another fundamental difference lies in the treatment effect estimate. Although sometimes used interchangeably, the HR used in time-to-first-event and the rate ratio used for total events analysis are not the same. 18 The rate in total events analysis is defined as the expected number of events in a small time interval and is estimated from the Poisson process with a robust SE in the Lin-Wei-Yang-Ying model. 19 This means that the treatment effect estimate is more robust to postrandomization selection bias due to population heterogeneity. However, total event analyses rely on different assumptions that may also be violated in HFpEF trials (eg, due to event clustering 20 ), and a direct replacement of the Cox regression with the total event analysis using the Lin-Wei-Yang-Ying method is not easily justifiable. Total event end points address a different therapeutic goal—the overall disease burden—and therefore, serve a different scientific objective. Hence, the choice between time-to-first event and total events analysis is not solely a statistical decision, but also a clinical one. On the other hand, replacing the Cox regression with SPOM does not necessitate a change of the end point or additional assumptions. The SPOM effectively replaces the assumption of proportionality of hazards with the assumption of proportionality of odds, which implies converging hazards over time. This is a more realistic assumption in large heterogeneity populations, similar to HFpEF trials where active treatment maintains consistent benefit while control patients experience early events and the control group becomes less frail over time, resulting in convergence of hazard rates of the 2 groups. The SPOM provides a different treatment effect measure, the SOR, which is not affected by postrandomization selection bias, is more robust to population heterogeneity, is directly on the survival curves as estimated by the Kaplan-Meier estimator, and is interpretable causally as the ratio of odds of being event-free in the active group compared with the control group. In contrast, HR is based on the more abstract mathematical concept of hazards and is frequently misinterpreted as a simple risk ratio, although it actually reflects the ratio of the instantaneous risk of an event among a selected subset of patients who have not yet experienced the event. In large heterogeneous populations, the SPOM outperforms the Cox regression in terms of statistical power and can be considered as an alternative primary analysis method in heart failure trials with time-to-first event end points. On the contrary, the SPOM will potentially lead to a reduction in statistical power in relatively homogeneous populations. As discussed earlier, in the case of the DELIVER trial, the proportionality of hazards assumption was violated, as reported in the primary publication. 10 On the contrary, in a similar HFpEF trial, FINEARTS-HF (Finerenone in Heart Failure With Mildly Reduced or Preserved Ejection Fraction) trial, 21 visual inspection of the Kaplan-Meier curves does not indicate a violation of the proportional hazards assumption (the curves in both curves are proportionally similar). This is further supported by the numerical equality between the rate ratio from the Lin-Wei-Yang-Ying model in the primary total event analysis (RR = 0.84, 95% CI, 0.74–0.95) and the HR from the Cox regression in the time-to-first event analysis (HR, 0.84 [95% CI, 0.76–0.94]). This suggests no reduction in the treatment effect estimate when using a method robust to population heterogeneity. We suspect that this population is less heterogeneous than DELIVER; therefore, the gain in efficiency with SPOM would not be substantial (but still likely advantageous to Cox regression). Another approach to addressing heterogeneity is to adjust for baseline prognostic factors in the Cox model and estimate the treatment effect conditional on these covariates. In this way, patients with the same risk according to baseline factors are compared, in theory preserving the balance created by randomization over time. Several methods exist for covariate adjustment, including novel approaches. 22 An interesting concept is the 5-step stratified testing and amalgamation routine for Cox regression, which uses baseline covariates to segment the heterogeneous trial population into subpopulations of prognostically homogeneous patients (risk strata). 23 The main problem with any covariate adjustment approach as a solution to risk heterogeneity is that substantial residual heterogeneity will likely remain—even with covariate adjustment—because key risk factors are not measured in the trial or may not even exist. This is evident in heart failure, where multivariable prognostic models demonstrate only moderate predictive ability—typically with a C-index around 0.70 (0.5 indicates no discrimination, 1.0 indicates perfect prediction) 24 —suggesting that most of the heterogeneity remains unexplained despite the use of current prognostic factors. With that said, our results show that even when adjusting for NT-proBNP in the dapagliflozin trials, SPOM consistently outperforms Cox regression also in estimating the conditional treatment effect. The survival odds model has some limitations. The model relies on the proportionality of odds assumption, which may also be violated in heterogeneous populations. Visual diagnostic tools can be applied to assess this assumption. We showed that in HFpEF-like trials, this assumption is likely to be violated to some extent. However, in heterogeneous populations, the proportional odds assumption is more likely to be met, offering a more robust model with higher statistical power than the Cox regression model, which similarly has violated assumptions. It should also be noted that the estimation of the SOR usually results in wider CIs than those of the HR from the Cox regression model. On the contrary, because of the selection bias leading to convergence towards 1 of HR in populations with large heterogeneity of risk, the Cox regression loses power compared with the SPOM, since the SOR is more robust to heterogeneity. Finally, this study has evaluated the applicability of SOR in heart failure trials only, in a setting where most patients do not experience events during follow-up (only around 10%–20%). Therefore, the conclusions may not be widely applicable in other settings, such as when the outcome of interest is very common or events accrue more rapidly. In populations with low heterogeneity, the SPOM, having a higher SE compared with the Cox model, is likely to lead to a decrease in statistical power, as no attenuation of the HR is expected in these populations. Therefore, the SPOM cannot replace the Cox regression model in all settings. Instead, population heterogeneity should be considered when choosing this model as the primary analysis method for time-to-first event end points. In the heart failure with preserved ejection fraction populations, the SPOM seems a particularly good fit. In all cases, the unexplained heterogeneity of the underlying population should be considered before using the SPOM as the primary analysis method. Future research should focus on estimating the degree of heterogeneity and determining the cutoff point at which increased heterogeneity reduces the power of the Cox regression compared with the SPOM. This substudy of the Dapagliflozin and Prevention of Adverse Outcomes in Heart Failure (DAPA-HF) randomized clinical trial investigates the association between cell adhesion molecules and adverse outcomes in chronic heart failure. Key Points Question Are cell adhesion molecules (vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 [VCAM-1] and intracellular adhesion molecule 1 [ICAM-1]) associated with adverse outcomes in chronic heart failure? Findings In this biomarker substudy of the Dapagliflozin and Prevention of Adverse-outcomes in Heart Failure (DAPA-HF) randomized clinical trial, 3051 participants had VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 levels measured. The risks of fatal and nonfatal outcomes were greater in those with higher VCAM-1 levels, even after adjustment for other known prognostic variables; there was no association between ICAM-1 levels and outcomes. Meaning Results suggest that VCAM-1 levels may reflect a distinct inflammatory/immune pathophysiological pathway in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Abstract Importance Vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1) and intracellular cell adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) are responsible for immune cell-cell interactions. Systemic levels of VCAM-1 are associated with incident heart failure (HF). Objectives To determine if VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 levels are associated with progression of established HF. Design, Setting, and Participants Participants enrolled in the biomarker substudy of the Dapagliflozin and Prevention of Adverse Outcomes in Heart Failure (DAPA-HF) randomized clinical trial had VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 levels measured at baseline and 12 months. The DAPA-HF trial was conducted at 410 sites in 20 countries. Patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) in New York Heart Association (NYHA) class II to IV with elevated natriuretic peptides were enrolled between February 15, 2017, and August 17, 2018, with final follow-up on June 6, 2019. Data were analyzed from January 2023 to January 2025. Interventions Dapagliflozin, 10 mg, once daily vs placebo. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was the composite of a worsening HF event or cardiovascular death. The associations between VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 levels at baseline and the primary outcome, its components, and all-cause death were analyzed using Cox proportional hazards regression models adjusted for known prognostic variables including estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), and high-sensitivity troponin T (hs-TnT), as well as high-sensitivity C-reactive protein. Results A total of 3051 participants (mean [SD] age, 67.2 [10.5] years; 2386 male [78.2%]) were included in this study. Mean (SD) follow-up time was 17.6 (5.2) months. The median (IQR) baseline VCAM-1 level was 997 (816.7-1218.8) ng/mL. Compared with patients with lower concentrations of VCAM-1, those with higher concentrations of VCAM-1 were older (mean [SD] age T3 vs T1, 69.7 [9.7] years vs 64.1 [10.7] years; P < .001), in worse NYHA class (T3 vs T1, NYHA class III/IV 35.6% [362 of 1017] vs 26.5% [269 of 1017]; P < .001), and had higher NT-proBNP (median [IQR] T3 vs T1, 2018 [1126-3753] pg/mL vs 1118 [693-1830] pg/mL) and hs-TnT (median [IQR] T3 vs T1, 24.7 [17.1-37.5] ng/L vs 16.6 [11.6-24.9] ng/L) concentrations, and lower eGFR (mean [SD] T3 vs T1, 58.4 [17.6] mL/min/1.73 m 2 vs 71.7 [18.0] mL/min/1.73 m 2 ). Patients in tertile 3 of VCAM-1, compared with tertile 1, had the highest risk of each outcome (eg, adjusted hazard ratio [HR] for primary outcome 1.40; 95% CI, 1.11-1.77; P = .004). ICAM-1 level was not associated with an elevated risk of any outcome. The benefit of dapagliflozin vs placebo in reducing the risk of the primary outcome was consistent across VCAM-1 tertiles: HR, 0.76 (95% CI, 0.54-1.06), 0.82 (95% CI, 0.59-1.12), and 0.77 (95% CI, 0.61-0.98) for tertiles 1, 2 and 3, respectively ( P for interaction = .93). There was no significant change in VCAM-1 level with dapagliflozin at 52 weeks. Conclusions and Relevance Results of this substudy of the DAPA-HF randomized clinical trial demonstrate that higher VCAM-1 levels, possibly reflecting a distinct inflammatory/immune pathophysiological pathway in HFrEF, were associated with worse outcomes, even after adjustment for conventional prognostic variables. Introduction Cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) belonging to the immunoglobulin superfamily include intracellular cell adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) and vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1), which mediate interactions between different cell types. 1 , 2 , 3 ICAM-1 expression is required for leukocyte interactions, including those that initiate inflammatory responses, and VCAM-1 is considered an endothelial cell protein that binds lymphocytes. Cardiovascular interest in these CAMs has been focused on their potential role in atherosclerosis. 1 , 2 , 3 However, VCAM-1 expression (but not ICAM-1 expression) is increased in ventricular cardiomyocytes from patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), compared with controls, and positively correlated with infiltration of T lymphocytes and other immune cells. 4 Similarly, VCAM-1 (but not ICAM-1) expression, was increased in the atrial tissue of patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), with greater expression in patients with lower left ventricular EF (LVEF). 5 ICAM-1 expression was found to be increased in myocardial biopsies from patients with HF and preserved EF (HFpEF) but not in those with HFrEF. 6 Circulating soluble isoforms of VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 are detectable in plasma and are thought to reflect proteolytic cleavage (ie, shedding) of the molecules. Systemic levels of VCAM-1 were predictive of incident HF in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). 7 Only 2 small (74 and 120 patients, respectively) single-center studies 8 , 9 published in 2003 and 2013, respectively, had previously attempted to examine the relationship between VCAM-1 and outcomes in HFrEF and gave conflicting results. Given these findings, in this post hoc analysis, we hypothesized that VCAM-1 (but not ICAM-1) would be associated with clinical outcomes among patients with established HFrEF and that this association would be independent of other biomarkers reflecting myocardial wall stress and injury. We tested this hypothesis in the biomarker substudy of the Dapagliflozin and Prevention of Adverse-outcomes in Heart Failure (DAPA-HF) randomized clinical trial, comparing dapagliflozin with placebo in patients with HFrEF. 10 We also tested the hypothesis that dapagliflozin would reduce circulating VCAM-1 concentration, because another sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor, empagliflozin, was shown to reduce VCAM-1 when incubated in vitro with skinned myocardial fibers isolated from left ventricular biopsies taken from patients with HFpEF. 11 Methods DAPA-HF was a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized clinical trial that compared dapagliflozin, 10 mg, once daily with placebo in patients with HFrEF. 10 Ethics committees for the 410 participating institutions in 20 countries approved the protocol, and patients gave written consent. Participation in the biomarker substudy was offered to patients in countries where local restrictions allowed prospective sample collection. This study followed the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials ( CONSORT ) reporting guidelines. Study Patients and Treatment Patients in New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class II to IV, with a LVEF of 40% or less and an elevated N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-pro-BNP) concentration, were eligible for study inclusion if receiving standard pharmacological and device therapy. The key exclusion criteria included type 1 diabetes and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . As required by the US Food and Drug Administration for participants in clinical trials, patients self-reported the following races and ethnicities: Asian, Black, White, and other, which included American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian/Puerto Rican, Black Hispanic, Caribbean, Hispanic, Latino, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, and South American Indian. Measurement of Vascular Adhesion Molecules VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 were measured at baseline and 12 months after randomization. Details of sample collection, assay, and assay performance are provided in eTable 1 in . Outcomes The primary outcome was the composite of a worsening HF event (HF hospitalization or urgent visit for HF requiring intravenous therapy) or cardiovascular death, whichever occurred first. We investigated the association between baseline CAM levels and the risk of the primary outcome, its components, all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, and stroke. We also examined the effect of dapagliflozin compared with placebo, according to baseline CAM level, on the primary end point and its components. Statistical Analysis Baseline CAM levels were categorized by tertiles. Baseline characteristics according to serum CAM levels are presented as frequencies and percentages for categorical variables and means with SD or medians with IQR for continuous variables. A nonparametric test for trend was used to examine for variation in continuous baseline characteristics across CAM tertiles. Correlations between adhesion molecules, NT-proBNP level, high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-TnT) level, and eGFR were determined using the Pearson correlation coefficient with log-transformed values as appropriate. The association between clinical and laboratory variables and ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 was examined using multivariable linear regression. Incidence rates for each outcome are presented per 100 person-years of follow-up. Event rates in each CAM tertile were estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method and compared using the log-rank test. The associations between baseline CAM levels and outcomes were analyzed using Cox proportional hazards regression models stratified by diabetes status and adjusted for a history of HF hospitalization (except the model for all-cause mortality). Further adjustment was performed for age, sex, heart rate, systolic blood pressure (BP), body mass index (BMI), ischemic HF etiology, LVEF, NYHA classification, AF, log NT-proBNP, log hs-TnT, log high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), and eGFR. The association between CAMs as continuous variables and outcomes was analyzed using restricted cubic splines with 5 knots using the median value as the reference. Both VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 were also dichotomized at or above/below an optimal cut point using the Youden method to maximize the product of the sensitivity and specificity of the cut point related to the primary composite outcome. 12 Kaplan-Meier survival curves were constructed to illustrate the likelihood of the primary outcome with levels above the cut point. A C index at 2 years was calculated for the primary outcome from a multivariable Cox model including clinically relevant variables known to be associated with this outcome (history of HF hospitalization, randomized treatment, age, sex, heart rate, systolic BP, BMI, ischemic HF etiology, LVEF, NYHA class, AF, and eGFR) and stratified by diabetes status. We compared the C index derived from this clinical model with the C index derived from a model after adding VCAM-1 or ICAM-1. For context, we also added NT-proBNP, hs-TnT, or hs-CRP to the model and calculated the respective C index. Finally, we tested whether VCAM-1 or ICAM-1 remained significant predictors in the model after adding these other biomarkers. 13 The effect of dapagliflozin compared with placebo on each outcome was calculated as hazard ratio (HR) and 95% CI derived from Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for a history of HF hospitalization and treatment assignment and stratified by baseline diabetes status (models for all-cause mortality did not include previous HF hospitalization). The effect of dapagliflozin on the primary outcome according to the level of CAM (analyzed as a continuous variable) was examined using a fractional polynomial analysis using the Stata mfpi command (StataCorp). The effect of dapagliflozin on CAM levels between baseline and 12 months is presented as a ratio of geometric means derived from a linear regression model adjusted for baseline values. All analyses were performed using Stata, version 17 (StataCorp). A 2-sided P value of <.05 was considered statistically significant (with no adjustment for multiplicity, given the exploratory nature of the analyses). Study data were analyzed from January 2023 to January 2025. Results Of the 4744 patients randomized in the DAPA-HF trial, 3051 (64.3%; mean [SD] age, 67.2 [10.5] years; 665 female [21.8%]; 2386 male [78.2%]) had a baseline measurement of VCAM-1 and ICAM-1. Discussion In this substudy of the DAPA-HF randomized clinical trial, we found that VCAM-1 was associated with nonfatal and fatal outcomes in patients with HF, and these associations persisted despite adjustment for other prognostic variables including LVEF, eGFR, NT-proBNP, and hs-TnT levels. Prior studies had shown that VCAM-1 levels are increased in patients with HF compared with controls. However, only 2 studies 8 , 9 examined the association between VCAM-1 and outcomes in HFrEF. The larger study 9 of the 2 included 120 patients with chronic HF, LVEF less than 45%, and coronary artery disease. Over 13 months of follow-up, 11 participants died, and 13 were hospitalized for HF. VCAM-1 was associated with all-cause mortality. However, this was not found in another study 8 of 74 patients with chronic HF and LVEF less than 50%. Results of our much larger cohort confirm that VCAM-1 was associated with outcomes in HFrEF. The explanation for high VCAM-1 levels in patients with HFrEF and why they are associated with HF hospitalization and death is uncertain. There was a decrement in kidney function across ascending tertiles of VCAM-1. It is not known whether VCAM-1 is cleared by the kidneys; although, in the general population, eGFR is inversely associated with circulating VCAM-1 concentration. 14 Nevertheless, in the present study, VCAM-1 was only modestly correlated with eGFR and remained predictive of outcomes, despite adjustment for eGFR. Interestingly, in people with metabolically healthy obesity, levels of VCAM-1 are not elevated compared with metabolically healthy lean controls (in contrast to ICAM-1). 15 We found that patients in the lowest tertile of VCAM-1 were less likely to have obesity than those in the highest tertile, a pattern opposite of what is observed with natriuretic peptides (and this pattern was not observed for ICAM-1). Another striking difference was the association between VCAM-1 levels and AF, with more than a 2-fold higher prevalence of AF in patients in the highest compared with lowest tertile of VCAM-1. In our study, this association persisted despite extensive adjustment for other important markers of severity of HF. In a prior study, 5 AF was associated with increased tissue expression of VCAM-1 (but not ICAM-1) in right atrial appendage samples obtained from 320 consecutive patients with (n = 61) and without (n = 259) AF undergoing cardiac surgery. In a supportive study, 16 rapid pacing of human atrial tissue slices led to a significant upregulation of VCAM-1 expression. The authors suggested that the endocardium was the source of VCAM-1. Furthermore, VCAM-1 was associated with the risk of incident AF over 20 years in a population-based cohort study, with a concentration-response–type relationship. Another potential source of VCAM-1 and a possible link between VCAM-1 and prognosis is inflammation of the myocardium. An association between serum VCAM-1 levels and myocardial inflammation was first shown in a small study 17 of 47 patients with nonischemic HF undergoing right ventricular biopsy. In 41% of those with elevated serum levels of VCAM-1, the myocardial biopsies showed increased lymphocytic infiltration and enhanced expression of the major histocompatibility complex antigens of class I/II indicating active inflammation. A recent larger study 4 examined 313 samples of ventricular myocardium obtained from 177 patients with HF (and 136 healthy controls). VCAM-1 expression was significantly higher in patients with HF, and VCAM-1 expression positively correlated with a variety of T cells and other immune cells, which were significantly elevated in the myocardial samples from patients with HF, compared with controls. Collectively, these studies suggest that circulating VCAM-1 and myocardial VCAM-1 expression are associated with myocardial immune infiltration (and that VCAM-1 may facilitate immune cell infiltration). Potentially relevant to a myocardial origin of VCAM-1 is a small study 18 demonstrating a rapid decrease in circulating levels of this biomarker after heart transplant, although the levels do not normalize. Elevated VCAM-1 levels may, therefore, be associated with worse outcomes in HFrEF because they reflect heightened immune and inflammatory activity, and downstream oxidative stress, in the myocardium. This hypothesis would also explain why the association is independent of natriuretic peptides, reflecting a distinct pathophysiological process. Importantly, this hypothesis suggests the inflammation reflected by VCAM-1 levels is focused in the myocardium because, although hs-CRP concentrations, reflecting systemic inflammation, were significantly higher among patients in the highest tertile of VCAM-1, the correlation between VCAM-1 and hs-CRP was weak. VCAM-1 reflects a more localized and specific role at the site of inflammation (ie, the myocardium) than hs-CRP. 19 , 20 What is not clear from these studies is whether cardiomyocytes, the endocardium, or vascular endothelial cells within the cardiac vasculature are sources of VCAM-1. In HFpEF, it has been suggested that VCAM-1 is linked to inflammation and microvascular dysfunction, processes thought to be important in the pathophysiology of that HF phenotype. 7 , 11 , 21 An additional potential source of VCAM-1 is the venous circulation. Colombo and colleagues 22 carried out a venous stress test (inflating a cuff around the upper arm above 30 mm Hg to increase venous pressure) in patients with HFrEF to mimic venous congestion. This led to an increase in VCAM-1 in venous blood drawn from the test arm, compared with the control arm. 22 Despite the suggestion that SGLT2 inhibition reduces myocardial VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 expression in vitro, 11 we did not find that dapagliflozin reduced circulating levels of either CAM, although our analysis was limited by having only 1 follow-up measurement after 12 months of treatment. However, our findings are in keeping with those from the EMPEROR (Empagliflozin Outcome Trial in Patients With Chronic Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction; Empagliflozin Outcome Trial in Patients With Chronic Heart Failure With Reduced Ejection Fraction) trials, in which 2 large-scale proteomic studies did not show differential expression of VCAM-1 or ICAM-1 after 3 months of treatment with empagliflozin or placebo. 23 , 24 Several other cell adhesion–related proteins were differentially expressed with empagliflozin with a 10-fold or greater increase as compared with placebo. Intracellular adhesion molecule 4 (ICAM-4) is a protein expressed on erythroid cells, and the increase in ICAM-4 is potentially consistent with the known erythropoietic effect of SGLT2 inhibitors. 25 Epithelial cell adhesion molecule (EpCAM) is thought to be important in the regeneration of kidney tubular cells in animal models and may account for some of the kidney protective effects of SGLT2 inhibitors. 26 Other differentially expressed proteins were carcinoembryonic antigen–related cell adhesion molecule 8, junctional adhesion molecule C, and cadherin-related family member 2; however, the potential link between the biological effect of these proteins and the clinical benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors has yet to be established. Experimentally, angiotensin II upregulates VCAM-1, and of interest, angiotensin II receptor blockade has been shown to reduce VCAM-1, 5 , 27 and a VCAM-1–neutralizing antibody attenuates angiotensin II-induced cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis. 28 Interestingly, we found that individuals receiving therapies targeting the renin-angiotensin system had lower VCAM-1 levels than those not taking these therapies. Similarly, atorvastatin has been shown to reduce VCAM-1 levels at 4 weeks and improve endothelial function in patients with heart failure. 29 We found lower VCAM-1 levels in those taking statins compared with those not taking statins. As stated previously, ICAM-1 levels were not elevated in this study, and this was also true for another CAM, activated leukocyte cell adhesion molecule, in a previous study in patients with HFrEF, supporting a VCAM-1–specific perturbation in HFrEF. 30 Limitations This study has some limitations. This was a post hoc exploratory analysis and is subject to confounding. The patients studied were selected according to trial inclusion and exclusion criteria. We did not have data on potentially upstream inflammatory cytokines. Biomarker collection was not performed in all participating countries, and not all randomized patients in the DAPA-HF trial were included. Therefore, there may be a degree of selection bias in these analyses and the results may not be generalizable to all patients with HFrEF or to patients with HFpEF. Conclusions In this substudy of the DAPA-HF randomized clinical trial, circulating VCAM-1 levels were associated with outcomes in HFrEF, even after adjustment for conventional prognostic variables including NT-proBNP, hs-TnT, and eGFR. VCAM-1 levels may reflect a distinct inflammatory/immune pathophysiological pathway in HFrEF. Dapagliflozin was of benefit across the range of VCAM-1 at baseline but did not reduce VCAM-1 level at 12 months.
